title: La cathédrale engloutie: Meyer and Ilić
work: La cathédrale engloutie, Préludes I, No. 10
question: How can the same piano sound like distant bells and a full cathedral organ?
intro: The piece opens with bare fifths in the manner of bells. The piano then imitates an organ, with C-major chords spread across the keyboard, before the music returns to a quiet echo. Marcelle Meyer and Ivan Ilić recorded La cathédrale engloutie in Paris, fifty years apart.

recordings.label: Marcelle Meyer, 1956
recordings.note: Meyer, a pupil of Cortot and Viñes, plays Debussy’s great chords with a full piano tone and carefully judged pedalling.

recordings.label: Ivan Ilić, 2006
recordings.note: Ilić’s Paris recording plays the chords with firm edges and uses flexible rhythm through the changes of pace.

passages.label: Opening fifths
passages.note: Bare Gs and Ds are played quietly. Rising fifths leave wide spaces between the notes.

passages.label: Triplets beneath rising chords
passages.note: Triplets enter beneath the rising chords, and the piano grows louder.

passages.label: Melody in C-major chords
passages.note: The organ-like tune is set in full C-major chords. Their top notes carry the melody above a deep bass.

passages.label: Return of the melody, pianissimo
passages.note: The great tune returns lower and pianissimo, over a moving bass. Debussy marks it as an echo of the earlier phrase.
